claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among the quinary, quaternary, and ternary FCC variants are primarily dictated by local lattice distortion and stacking-fault-energy variations caused by chemical ordering.
Constituent count alone is not the primary explanation for the differences in deformation and failure behavior.
Variations in stacking fault energy modify the balance between dislocation slip and deformation twinning.
Changes in the balance between dislocation slip and twinning alter work hardening and ductility.
The quinary alloy and all corresponding equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets are single-phase FCC after identical thermomechanical processing.
Paired mechanical tests with EBSD and TEM can compare dislocation configurations and deformation-twin densities among the alloys.
Room-temperature testing at identical strain rates, specimen geometries, and processing histories provides a controlled compositional comparison.
Removing one or more elements from the quinary alloy alters local chemical ordering.
Changes in local chemical ordering affect the magnitude and spatial variability of lattice distortions and stacking-fault energetics.
Reduced-component quaternary and ternary alloys have a higher effective stacking fault energy than the quinary alloy.
Higher stacking fault energy suppresses mechanical twinning and favors dislocation slip.
The quinary alloy has more pronounced local lattice distortions and a lower average stacking fault energy than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Enhanced twinning and complex dislocation interactions in the quinary alloy improve strain hardening and ductility.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit lower deformation-twin density and reduced dislocation entanglement.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit diminished strain hardening and potentially lower tensile strength and ductility.
The equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi alloy processed under the same conditions is the experimental baseline.
The predictions are restricted to room-temperature plastic deformation under controlled strain rate, specimen size, machine compliance, and thermomechanical history.
Comparable ordering-related mediators, deformation mechanisms, and mechanical properties across the subsets and quinary baseline would falsify the proposed primary-cause explanation.

contradictions.description: The broad prediction that ternary subsets may have lower strength and ductility than the quinary baseline is not consistent with cited record PMC5893566, which reports that CrCoNi has strength and plastic deformation superior to CrMnFeCoNi and attributes this to a slip-triggered FCC-to-HCP transformation.
